source.title: On improving deep learning generalization with adaptive sparse connectivity
source.authors: Shiwei Liu; D. Mocanu; Mykola Pechenizkiy

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares generalization of intrinsically sparse MLPs with fully connected MLPs using a different architecture comparison from the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-accuracy comparisons on 15 datasets and learning-curve comparisons on four datasets. These results bear on architecture and generalization, but none of the listed versions specifically covers sparse adaptive connectivity in MLPs on these datasets. The paper also describes a neuron-removal experiment in Figure 1, but reports only one dataset and does not state exact values; it is not a test of a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study compares adaptive sparse MLPs with dense MLPs, but tests none of V1–V8. It does not compare convolutional networks or establish learned spatial locality (V3); neuron pruning is neither a width sweep beyond interpolation (V2) nor removal of memorized training examples (V8). The other versions' interventions and measures are also absent.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: SET and NPSET can improve generalization over fully connected counterparts, and NPSET reduces parameters while retaining competitive accuracy. This is the authors' interpretation; Table 2 does not show superiority on every dataset, and the learning-curve comparison covers only four datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The comparison concerns sparse evolutionary training and neuron pruning versus directly trained fully connected MLPs; it does not use the claim versions' interventions. No original method is reproduced.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset changes the reported maximum-accuracy comparison; learning curves are shown only for four datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports selected maximum test accuracies for adaptive sparse and dense MLPs on 15 datasets. NPSET exceeds Direct FC on 12 datasets, ties on arcene, and is slightly lower on gisette and RELATHE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive sparse MLP training can outperform directly trained dense MLPs with the final pruned hidden-layer sizes on limited-sample classification datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report smaller training–test accuracy gaps for SET and NPSET than for Dense-MLP on four datasets without explicit regularization. On Yale, Dense-MLP reaches zero training loss and 100% training accuracy while the sparse models do not fit training data perfectly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive sparse connectivity can reduce training–test accuracy gaps relative to dense MLPs with the initial SET hidden-layer sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 reports maintained or improved accuracy after removing low-output-degree hidden neurons on Lung-discrete.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some low-output-degree hidden neurons can be removed from a trained sparse MLP without reducing classification accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: ICML 2019 Workshop on Understanding and Improving Generalization in Deep Learning (PMLR 97)
record.problems: The paper focuses only on MLPs and limited-sample datasets. Exact learning-curve gap values are not given in the text, and the curves are displayed for only four datasets. Results report maximum accuracy, not uncertainty estimates. Some parenthetical differences in Table 2 appear inconsistent with displayed values or refer to another baseline.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 also lists NPSET, 1st NPSET, 2nd NPSET, and Direct SET results on all 15 datasets. These method comparisons were omitted to keep the extraction focused on sparse versus fully connected generalization; the table's comparisons with Direct FC-MLP are included above. Figure 1's neuron-removal accuracy curve is not extracted because exact values are figure-only and it does not bear on a listed version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level random-label test performance, and coexistence with natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Test error across widths beyond the width needed for zero training error; no interpolation-threshold analysis.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, spatial locality, and initialization from trained convolutional networks. Adaptive sparsity alone does not test these comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning scope, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes to the training recipe.
Effects of adding or removing dropout, dropout strength, training-set size interactions, and augmentation or weight-decay interactions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized training examples versus equally many random examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked to V1–V8; cannot_determine denotes that their measures cannot establish a listed effect, not that the reported method comparisons are unreadable. Table 2 parenthetical differences consistently use SET as baseline, rather than Direct FC; most apparent inconsistencies in R16–R30 arise from the extraction changing that baseline. R8 contains a genuine arithmetic discrepancy in the source table. Direct FC in Table 2 uses the final pruned hidden-layer sizes, whereas Dense-MLP in Figure 2 uses SET's initial hidden-layer sizes. The selected maximum accuracies are method-performance summaries and should not serve as claim-verdict rows. No additional result bearing on a listed version is missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; no random-label training.
Widening beyond interpolation and test-error behavior across widths.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks on image datasets, local connectivity, and convolutional initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and optimizer tuning.
Large-batch training and batch-size-dependent generalization gaps.
Dropout effects and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
